zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical coverage was cross-checked after the independent scan reading against Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (CC BY 4.0): https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html . Its normalized headwords were not used as diplomatic authority.

lines.note: Umigoshi and umigoshini mean across, or on the other side of, the sea. The headword has mi, matching the repeated form; OCR Vnigoxi is corrected from the visible m.

runs.text: do mar, ou paßando o mar. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese permits both the far side of the sea and crossing it. The paragraph sign introduces the Japanese example, whose umigoshi is physically divided after Vmigoxi-.
The example says that one knows a mountain is there, although it cannot be seen across the sea, because the sun has set behind it. Posto que begins the concessive Portuguese translation below.

runs.text: não parece monte da outra parte do mar, pare-

lines.note: The concessive clause says no mountain appears on the other side of the sea. The visible pare- is the first part of parece and remains divided at the printed row ending.

runs.text: ce que o auera pois ſe pos o ſol.

lines.note: Completes the inference that there must be a mountain because the sun has set. Historical auera and unaccented pos are retained as printed.
Umigiwa is the edge or shore of the sea, directly glossed borda do mar.
Umisuzume is identified simply as a small seabird. The gloss does not justify assigning a more precise modern species.
Umizura denotes the surface of the sea; the doubled z spelling is retained without imposing a modern romanization.
Umore, umoruru, umoreta describes becoming buried or covered. The Portuguese objects and covering materials are specified on the next row.

runs.text: a erua, ou paos com a neue, terra, &c.

lines.note: Grass or wood becomes covered by snow, earth, and similar material. The scan separates a erua; it is the Portuguese article plus noun, not the OCR compound aerua.
The paragraph sign, omitted by OCR, begins the example: when heavy snow falls, the plants of fields and mountains are buried. Vôyuqi is retained with the visible circumflex.
Trees, too, become buried; vzzumoruru supplies an alternative verb. Cho- begins the Portuguese chovendo translation across the line break.

runs.text: uendo muita neue ficão as eruas, & aruores

lines.note: Completes Chouendo and describes abundant snow leaving grasses and trees covered. The clause continues with enterradas below.
The vegetation is buried underneath the snow. A new item then extends the verb to silting or filling up.

runs.text: ou irſe entulhando acaua com terra, ou ciſco,

lines.note: The filling-up sense concerns a ditch becoming clogged with earth or debris. The printed acaua is retained rather than normalized to a modern spelling or spacing.
The earth or debris falls into the ditch. This short continuation completes the preceding definition.

runs.text: Pao enterrado, ou cuberto de ter-

lines.note: Umoregi is buried wood or timber covered by soil. The Portuguese terra is divided after ter- at the right rule.

runs.text: ra como os que ficão caidos nos valles, & cu-

lines.note: The example is wood that falls in valleys and becomes covered with earth. Cu- continues as bertos on the next row.
Bertos completes cubertos: the fallen wood has already become covered with earth. The physical word division is retained.

runs.text: Poço de que ſe não tira ja agoa, ou

lines.note: Umorei is a well from which water is no longer drawn. The following alternative explains the well as nearly filled with soil.

runs.text: que eſtà ja quaſi entulhado com a terra.

lines.note: Completes the definition of an abandoned or filled-in well. The printed eſtà and ja are retained without modernizing their accents.

runs.text: Auer, ou não auer: ſi, ou

lines.note: Umu is explained by ari nashi, existence and nonexistence, and by Portuguese yes or no. These alternatives underlie the idioms that follow.
Umu ni mo kakawarazu introduces indifference or failure to engage; the alternative expression begins umu- and continues below.
Umu no henji mo sezu means making no yes-or-no reply. The Portuguese explicitly describes not giving either answer.

runs.text: ou de não, ou não tendo deuer com o que lhe di-

lines.note: The Portuguese adds the sense of paying no regard to what someone says. Di- continues into zem on the next physical row.
After completing dizem, the next example describes not distinguishing yes from no. Wakimayezu is a negative verb form, not a malformed modern spelling.

runs.text: Diz ſe de hum homem neſcio que

lines.note: Shirazu is an alternative to wakimayezu. The Portuguese applies the idiom to a foolish person and continues its explanation below.

runs.text: não entende, nem percebe as couſas. ¶

lines.note: The foolish person neither understands nor perceives things. V- starts another example with umu; the terminal hyphen belongs to that Japanese fragment.
Umu no hedate wo shirazu means not knowing the distinction between existence and nonexistence or yes and no. Idem refers to the preceding foolish-person gloss.
Un is first glossed victory, illustrated by un wo hiraku or eru, obtaining success. This begins the N subdivision after the internal heading.
The first example means attaining victory. The next says fortune is in heaven; aye- begins ayete on the following physical row.
The maxim continues with a prohibition on retreating. The Portuguese begins its rendering as fortune or victory, continuing below.

runs.text: vitoria està no ceo, guardai vos não fujais, ou

lines.note: The Portuguese places victory in heaven and warns the listener not to flee. The visible grave accent in està is restored without changing the provisional st allograph.

runs.text: não vos afaſteis. ¶ Item, Fortuna, ou vẽ-

lines.note: The warning continues: do not withdraw. A second item then glosses un as fortune or luck, with ventura divided between rows.
Un ni makasuru means entrusting oneself to fortune or taking a chance. Auenturar- is visibly continued by ſe below.
After completing aventurar-se, un ga kiwamaru describes good fortune reaching its end. The Portuguese noun phrase continues on the next line.

runs.text: boa dita, ou ventura de alguem. ¶

lines.note: The gloss completes the ending of a person's good luck. Vn- starts the next expression, un ga katamuku, without merging the physical rows.
Un ga katamuku means good fortune declining. The Portuguese describes a gradual ending rather than the completed loss in the preceding expression.
Un ga tsukuru is another expression for fortune coming to an end. The paragraph sign separates this example from the preceding one.
Unagasu, also fure unagasu, means proclaiming or giving an alarm or notice. The alternate form is Japanese, introduced by Latin vel.

The main text completes the sense of giving an alarm or warning. The displaced far-right chamar, &c. belongs in meaning to the crier definition on the next row; its opening mark and physical placement are preserved rather than reordered.

runs.text: O q̃ tem este officio de apregoar, ou

lines.note: Unagaxi here names the person whose office is proclaiming or calling out. The sentence is completed by the displaced chamar, &c. on the preceding physical row.

Unagi is an eel, glossed Inguia in italic Portuguese. The far-right dez, ou 12. P. is displaced completion of the age range under Vnaico below; it is kept on this physical row, with the separate opening mark and upright poetic-use label.

runs.text: Minino de dous, & tres annos atè

lines.note: Unaiko denotes a child, with the Portuguese range beginning at two or three years and continuing to ten or twelve in the displaced material above. The visible initial V corrects OCR Nnaico.
Unaidori is equated with hototogisu. The Portuguese begins a bird description that continues at the top of the second column; the omitted initial V is restored from the scan.

runs.text: ſaro que canta triste no verão.

lines.note: Completes paſſaro across the column break and describes the bird as singing mournfully in summer. It belongs to Vnaidori, not to the following pine entry.
Unaimatsu is a small pine just beginning to grow. The scan reads cre-, not OCR ere-, at the physical division of crecer.
Cer completes crecer, growing. The final upright P. marks poetic usage and is not part of the italic Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: Fio do lombo entre os dous ombros.

lines.note: Unaji is described as the ridge or line of the back between the shoulders. The historical definition is retained without substituting a modern anatomical gloss.
Uname is equated with Mevji and glossed as a cow. The roman synonym is retained as printed rather than regularized from the familiar modern word for female cattle.
Unatare, unataruru, unatareta means drooping or inclining oneself. The reflexive Portuguese verb is divided before ſe.
The example describes the cheeks drooping. Fôga supplies the cheek subject, and the Portuguese translation continues below.

runs.text: ou maçãas do rosto caidas, & derrubadas. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: The gloss specifies cheeks or cheekbones fallen or drooping. Itẽ introduces a further transitive sense on the next row.
The next sense is to lower or incline something; the Japanese example starts lowering the head. Cǒbeuo is retained with the visible caron and attached object particle.
Ruru completes unataruru. The Portuguese explicitly renders the action as inclining or lowering the head.
Unazzuki, unazzuku, unazzuita is nodding the head. The following line specifies assent or showing comprehension.
The nod signals agreement or understanding. Cedendo completes concedendo across the physical line break.

runs.text: Certa laya de Mochis, ou bolinhos fei-

lines.note: Unbin is a particular kind of mochi, explained as small cakes. Mochis is a Japanese food term embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Tos completes feitos: the cakes are made of rice. This short row completes Unbin and is not a separate entry.
Unbu is equated with kumo and kiri, cloud and mist. The final upright S. marks written usage.
Vnbut is followed by the preferred alternative Vnmot, then atatakana mono, a warm thing. The intervening potiùs is one italic Latin word, not Japanese tiù; the spurious mixed typography is corrected.
The Portuguese gives warmth or a warm thing, confirming the preceding Japanese explanation without supplying a modernized headword.
Unca is explained through clouds and haze, kumo and kasumi. The Portuguese adds vapours on the next row.

runs.text: ou vapores. ¶ Item, Couſa muita em quã-

lines.note: After completing the weather sense, the next item introduces a large quantity of something. Quã- is the printed abbreviated beginning of quantidade.

runs.text: tidade como gente de guerra. Vt,

lines.note: Tidade completes quantidade, with troops as the example of a multitude. The scan has a single tidade, correcting OCR tida de; teqiua begins the Japanese illustration.
The enemy appeared like clouds or mist, meaning in great numbers. The Portuguese inimigos is split after ini without a secure printed terminal hyphen, so none is supplied.

runs.text: migos como nuuens, ou vapores. i, em gran-

lines.note: The comparison is explicitly explained as a great multitude. Gran- continues into de on the next row.
De multidão completes grande multidão, the figurative sense of the cloud comparison.
Uncacu is paraphrased kumo no marebito and glossed as court nobles. Cũgues is the Japanese court-rank term embedded in Portuguese, and no- continues into nobres.
The nobles belong to the Dairi court. Guecqei vnca- begins a further Japanese expression with the same meaning; Dairi occurs within the Portuguese explanation.
Cu completes uncacu in the compound expression. Idem sends the reader back to the court-noble definition.
Unchǔ, kumo no uchi, means within the clouds. The final upright S. is the written-register label; the vowel mark on the headword is a visible caron.
Unda is glossed as a letter or written message. The final upright S. marks the word as literary or written usage.
Undei is explained literally as cloud and mud. The Portuguese develops this into the contrast between heaven and earth.
The figurative comparison is heaven versus earth. Tenchi undei- begins the illustrative Japanese expression, continued below.
No hedate ja completes the Japanese statement that the difference is like that between heaven and earth. The Portuguese likewise begins a great-difference comparison.
Completes the comparison from heaven to earth. This short continuation belongs with the undei idiom.
Undô is related to carrying and moving, hakobi and ugoku, and here glossed specifically as circular motion. The narrow scope of the printed definition is retained.
Ten no undô illustrates the motion of the heavens. The final S. is upright written-register label within the line, not italic Portuguese prose.
Undon is said to be pronounced udon, with a reference to the earlier entry. Vdon is the cited Japanese form embedded in the Portuguese pronunciation statement.

runs.text: Margem que fica entre rego, & rego.

lines.note: Une is the raised margin or ridge between furrows. The agricultural example begins on the next row.
Une wo yaru or une wo tatsuru means making these ridges. The printed paragraph sign omitted by OCR is restored before the example.

runs.text: estas margens. ¶ Item, per met. Em

lines.note: After completing the ridge-making gloss, a figurative extension applies the ridge shape to manual work. Per met. is preserved as the printed explanatory abbreviation.

runs.text: algũas obras de mãos fazer hũa maneira de

lines.note: The manual-work sense concerns making a kind of raised border or fold. The clause continues on the next row.
The border or fold is raised. This completes the figurative sense of une before the separate cord-making term below.

runs.text: Modo de tecer cordões deixando hũas

lines.note: Uneuchi is a way of weaving cords so that some parts stand higher. The scan shows plural hũas, correcting OCR hũa-; no line-end hyphen is printed there.
Some portions of the cord are higher than others. Vnevchino begins the compound example continued on the next line.

Uneuchi no ſaguevo refers to sword cords made with raised portions. The first glyph of ſaguevo has a damaged upper hook: its tall stem and detached rightward fragment, compared with local roman long-s types, favour ſ over OCR I or a dotted i. The reading remains a nonblocking glyph caveat. The Portuguese dependurauão is continuous in the scan, correcting the OCR space.
The cords were attached to catanas and made in this manner. Catanas is a Japanese object term embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Unguenberi is the edging on tatami of the Dairi court. Tatamis and Dairi are embedded Japanese terms in the Portuguese definition.
Unget is explained as cloud and moon, kumo and tsuki. The printed final t is retained, and S. is the upright written-usage label.
Ungin means freight or carriage charges. Ungin wo nasu illustrates paying those charges; the Portuguese verb is completed by its object on the next row.
Fretes completes pagar fretes, paying freight. The signature and catchword sharing this horizontal band are separated as furniture; the word itself remains under its original body-line ID.
